items.title: Landlady to 9/11 hijackers reveals their links to alleged Saudi spy
items.summary: A woman who rented out homes to two al-Qaeda members speaks publicly for the first time - to the BBC.
items.content:
Holly Ratchford still cannot believe that the man who moved into the residential complex she once managed would go on to be accused of involvement in the darkest day in recent US history.

"It's almost impossible for me to wrap my head around who he said he was, and who he really is. I still struggle with that," she tells the BBC.

The man, Omar al-Bayoumi - a Saudi in his early 40s - moved to the complex in San Diego, California, with his family in September 1999.

The new resident at number 152 Parkwood Apartments quickly became a regular at Ratchford's pool parties. "He was always so bubbly and smiling," she recalls, "and just very, very friendly."

A few months later, Bayoumi would introduce Ratchford to two apparently unassuming, "polite" men, who would also become her neighbours.

The pair would become infamous for hijacking American Airlines flight 77, and crashing it into the Pentagon, in the 9/11 attacks.

Ratchford has been haunted by her connection to these three men for the past 25 years. She feels she was taken in by Bayoumi from the start.

"Whenever I had parties he would come and be a part of the activities," she recalls, adding that his family would invite her in for food.

But Bayoumi, the one-time resident of 152 Parkwood, is now at the centre of the $1 trillion (£733bn) lawsuit brought against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia by several thousand families of victims and as well as survivors of 9/11.

On 11 September 2001, four passenger aircraft were hijacked by 19 members of the Islamist extremist network, al-Qaeda. In addition to the crash at the Pentagon - the US military's headquarters near Washington DC - two planes were flown into the twin towers of the World Trade Center in New York, causing both buildings to collapse. A fourth crashed in a field in Pennsylvania, following resistance from passengers on board.

In all, almost 3,000 people were killed, including about 300 firefighters and other emergency workers at the World Trade Center.

Bayoumi is alleged to have facilitated the 9/11 plot through the support he provided for the first two hijackers to arrive in the US - Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar - who lived at Parkwood for several months prior to the attacks.

The federal judge in the 9/11 families' lawsuit in New York found a year ago that the evidence created "a reasonable inference" that Bayoumi and a Saudi diplomat based in the US had been "co-ordinating with the Saudi government when providing assistance to the hijackers".

The judge's ruling has allowed the families' case to move forward. Saudi Arabia is appealing it and, together with Bayoumi, has always denied the allegations.

Ever since the attacks, Bayoumi has been the subject of reporting and speculation.

Ratchford - who saw him interacting with the hijackers and witnessed him providing a crucial act of support for them - has given a sealed declaration to the New York court.

After unwittingly becoming embroiled in the investigation into what the US government has described as "the most egregious criminal act on American soil in modern history", she moved about as far from humanity as you can get in the United States.

I tracked her down to the high desert in the western US - rattlesnake country. She told me she avoided the news, and definitely did not speak to journalists. But, to my surprise, she agreed to talk.

Her interview with me casts doubt on the version of events Bayoumi has told police, the FBI and the New York court, and features in the BBC Radio 4 podcast, Intrigue: A 9/11 Story , and an upcoming BBC Panorama, 9/11: The Saudi Connection .

Twenty-five years on from the deadliest terror attack in history, Jane McMullen asks why thousands of grieving families are still fighting for answers.

In early 1999, Ratchford landed on her feet. Life before then had been untethered - she had moved around, been married, pregnant and divorced before she was 21. But now, aged 27, she had a job she loved and a home.

As the new property manager of Parkwood Apartments, a squat complex of 175 low-rise apartments and townhouses in the San Diego suburbs, she says she excelled. Properties were never empty for long. But it was not the paperwork, nor the healthy pay check, that made the job a dream, it was the people.

Ratchford not only worked at Parkwood, she lived there too. Her clients were also her neighbours. And many were more than that - she says they became her friends.

"I always told my staff: 'You make them feel like this is their home, and they'll stay,'" she recalls.

As Ratchford made her mark at Parkwood, she was happy and secure in the world she had built - a world in which she knew everyone and everything.

Omar al-Bayoumi moved into Parkwood claiming to be a mature student.

"I knew he was going to school. I'm not sure, other than that, what he did," Ratchford says.

More than two decades later, declassified FBI documents and court filings would reveal that Bayoumi's studies had, in effect, come to a halt in 1998. He was spending much more time organising religious activities in the Muslim community, which he often videotaped.

His constant filming, and his inquiring questions, aroused suspicions.

"It was a general consensus of people in the San Diego Muslim community that Bayoumi was an operative of the Saudi intelligence service," Richard Lambert, who led the city's FBI office investigation after 9/11, tells me.

But it was not Ratchford's business to pry. What mattered to her was whether he could pay the rent. And he could.

The FBI would later discover he was being paid about $90,000 (£55,600 at the time) a year.

The Bayoumi who Ratchford saw was captured on his never-before-broadcast home movies - throwing a ball around with his family by the Parkwood pool, laughing when it drifted into the water.

Another video reveals him on an excursion to Las Vegas with his family. Wearing a floral shirt, he points out the rollercoaster by the New York, New York hotel casino.

"I bought into everything that he told me. I really thought that's how he was," Ratchford says.

But that version of Bayoumi is at odds with the man who emerges from other videos.

In summer 1999, Bayoumi filmed the United States Capitol in Washington DC from different angles, noting a "plan", and turning the camera on himself to deliver a reporter-style commentary.

The 9/11 families' lawyers allege he was surveilling the building as a potential target for the attacks. The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia maintains it is a tourist video.

In his August 2025 judgement, the New York judge found that "all the Court can conclude" from the video is that Bayoumi "visited Washington DC and that he filmed the city".

On 3 February 2000, Bayoumi brought two young men into Ratchford's San Diego rental office. In an obvious hurry, she says, he perched on the filing cabinet as he told her that the two men were from his mosque and were staying with him while they looked for a place to rent.

"There was absolutely nothing unusual about them. They were nice, they were polite," she recalls.

The two men spoke no English, but Bayoumi took charge. Ratchford says he asked her what the two men would need to show in order to qualify for a Parkwood apartment.

"They didn't meet the income criteria at all, or the bank account. They had none of that," she tells me.

But the two men did have several thousand dollars in cash. Bank records show that, the following day, Bayoumi took them to the nearest bank and helped them open an account.

Back at Ratchford's office on the third day, he figured a way around the problematic income criterion. He would co-sign their lease - becoming the legal guarantor for their apartment.

The rental agreement shows Bayoumi's multiple signatures. He was their guarantor, their friend, their emergency contact, and his Parkwood home was listed as their current address.

Without further delay, the two men moved into number 150, a one-bed apartment just a few doors down from Bayoumi's poolside townhouse.

The two men Bayoumi was assuming legal responsibility for - Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar - would become 9/11 hijackers.

Hazmi and Mihdhar stayed in their apartment until the end of May that year, and then moved out. Ratchford thought no more about it.

Sixteen months later, as America reeled in shock and grief in the days following the 9/11 attacks, she says a woman called asking her for a rental reference for them. Without thinking, she rattled off their details.

But the woman was not a property agent - she was a reporter.

Her next question shook Ratchford: "Did you know that they were two of the terrorists that flew their plane into the Pentagon?"

On 14 September 2001, two special agents interviewed Ratchford in her Parkwood office.

She gave them Bayoumi's guarantor form, triggering an investigation into the man they would come to see as the main facilitator of the two hijackers' lives in San Diego.

Richard Lambert, now retired from the FBI and working as a consultant to the 9/11 families' lawsuit, says "as we began to identify the hijackers' associates, what became clear is that there was a network headed up by Omar al-Bayoumi".

items.title: What tariffs will really cost Canadians and Americans
items.summary: Households and businesses have become used to tariffs impacting the cost of living for more than year now, so what will change now?
items.content:
A raft of new tariffs have been announced during the latest escalation of the trade war between the US and Canada.

The North American neighbours have been locked in a bitter economic conflict since US President Donald Trump launched his flagship trade policy on his return to the White House.

This week saw the latest move by the Canadians with Prime Minister Mark Carney imposing retaliatory import taxes on a host of US goods, after Trump threatened hikes of his own.

As the dust settles in this tit-for-tat tariff row, what will be affected most on both sides of the border?

If Trump's threat to raise tariffs on Canadian vehicles from 25% to 50% from 1 January 2027 becomes a reality, then that would deal a further blow to the automotive industry.

Cars, trucks and parts are among the main goods traded between the US, Canada and Mexico, with the manufacturing sector and supply chains stretching across borders.

Despite previous tariffs increasing costs for manufacturers, car dealerships have absorbed the "lion's share" to date, according to Bernard Yaros, lead economist at Oxford Economics.

"But that cushion is wearing thin," he adds. "The recently threatened 50% tariffs on Canadian autos, trucks, and car parts would feed through to consumer prices more readily than before."

Yaros thinks higher costs on imports to the US could accelerate a trend of manufacturers prioritising luxury cards, SUVs and pick-up trucks and push up prices in the used-car market if supplies of new but less-expensive vehicles becomes tight.

Carney has decided not to match Trump's 50% tariff threat so far, but a 25% import tax on certain American vehicles has been in place since last year.

Construction materials such as steel, aluminium as well as lumber wood have had tariffs in place before the latest escalation, though Canada has now matched US rates on the metals at 50%.

Carney has also imposed import taxes on several US wood products, such as plywood, and even screws used to fix timber together.

That means building firms that import such materials will face higher costs and may choose to pass those on through higher prices - pushing up the cost of homes, for example.

The Forest Products Association of Canada says tariffs would "raise costs on both sides of the border", while on the US side, Bill Owens, chairman of the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) urged Trump to make building materials exempt from his tariff agenda due to an "ongoing housing affordability crisis".

"Building material tariffs heighten market uncertainty, strain supply chains and increase construction costs," he says.

In 2024 the US imported $23bn (C$32bn, £17bn) worth of wood products, with almost half from Canada, according to a US Congress report.

But the so-called "lumber wars" between the nations on soft wood used in housebuilding are not new and stretch back decades.

Trump says Canada wants 'benefits' of being US state after trade talks collapse

Carney faces crucial test after walking away from Trump's deal

A key factor in this episode of the tariff war is the volume of household items that have been specifically targeted as opposed to raw materials.

Carpets, washing machines, furniture, fridges and even knives, forks and spoons are set to have tariffs applied by Canada.

While there is a risk prices on some of those goods being imported from the US could rise, the more likely scenario is that consumers will turn to domestic alternatives, according to Bradley Saunders, North America economist at Capital Economics.

He says Carney's latest move has intentionally targeted goods where Canadians can "shift to domestic suppliers instead".

"Like hair care products, you really can just buy that domestically instead," he adds.

Saunders explains Carney's response aims to "minimise the impact on Canadian households as much as possible by picking very fungible goods".

The Budget Lab at Yale, which monitors the impact of US government policy on the economy, says it anticipates seeing marginal increases in furnishing and other household equipment for Americans largely due to tariffs on lumber and other materials.

There may not be a material impact on alcohol prices, but it's clear the trade war has had an impact on Canadians' choice of drink.

Many provinces in the country banned US alcohol sales last year in response to previous tariffs, with the American wine and spirits industry saying exports to the country dropped more than 70%.

Carney asked the provinces to restore US alcohol to the shelves during trade talks, but now that they have collapsed, it's likely the ban will return.

Saunders says there's been a big push to "buy Canadian" from politicians and it has been successful when it comes to the strong stuff.

"That's really had an impact on the American alcohol industry," he adds.

Saskatchewan and Alberta are ​the only provinces that still sell ​American alcohol, but the former has announced its own 50% charge on US imported booze, set to kick in on 8 September, when the wider Canadian tariffs do.

While tariffs can end up hitting consumers in the pocket, there are other impacts on households.

Import taxes can complicate trade for businesses that have cross-border supply. As well as the higher costs, the uncertainty created by the trade war could put off investment plans and stunt job creation.

Saunders suggests the biggest impact on households may not just be through prices, but job losses instead.

"If you're, let's say, a bespoke furniture producer in BC [British Columbia], you're now facing a 50% tariff on your exports to the US - that could really shut the business down. I think that would be more the direct impact on households as opposed to these retaliatory measures."

Canada's forest industry employs almost 200,000 people and has called on the government to boost domestic demand through federal housing programs to make greater use of Canadian wood, though it admits "no support package can replace reliable access to our largest export market".

When it comes to US, consumers are unlikely to see much of a difference in terms of the cost of living as result of this latest battle with Canada, but frictions to trade can have longer-term economic impacts.

Such tensions also feed into concerns over the free-trade agreement between Canada, the US and Mexico, known as the USMCA. Both Canada and Mexico have said they want the USMCA extended for another 16 years, but the US has said it will not renew in its current form.

Despite the deal remaining operational, tariffs risk putting off talks in the near future, creating more uncertainty for cross-border trade.

John Iselin, associate director at the Budget Lab at Yale, estimates the cost will only be about $3 per American household on average, but when taking into account Trump's wider trade war with the rest of the world, and particularly China, the added costs rise to about $1,000 for the average family.

"It's hard to view this particular instance with Canada in isolation because we've had similar interactions with a range of other countries, all of which makes doing business harder. It's just another in a series of tariff shocks."

items.title: Canada poaches dozens of top US researchers for its universities
items.summary: Researchers in fields like climate and medicine are being lured north by new research funding.
items.content:
Canada is hiring dozens of researchers from US universities, including top research institutions such as Harvard, as its relationship with its neighbour continues to sour.

More than three-quarters of the 64 professors who are moving to Canada from around the world will come from the US. They will receive funding from a pool of C$504m ($362m; £268m) for research in fields such as climate change and medicine under a new government programme.

US President Donald Trump's administration has accused universities of being dominated by left-wing ideology and diversity policies, and of failing to tackle alleged campus antisemitism.

The BBC contacted the White House and US Department of Education.

The administration has also frozen federal research grants for many different institutions and groups that they have argued were wasteful , external . That uncertainty is helping lure researchers elsewhere.

Meanwhile, Canada is asserting itself more on the global stage while it pushes back against the US in their escalating trade war, which reached a major turning point over tariffs recently .

One climate researcher told the BBC that he was relocating to Canada in part because his work in the US had become more difficult in recent years.

Seth Guikema, a climate resiliency researcher at the University of Michigan and one of the 48 US researchers relocating to Canada, said he had decided to approach Canadian institutions last year in search of opportunities.

"The funding environment in the US for anything related to climate and resilience has become challenging," Guikema said. "I was looking for a good intellectual home where I could have practical impact."

Over the next eight years, Guikema said he would use C$8m to research tools for better preparing for natural hazards, like storms and wildfires, at the University of Western Ontario.

The University of Michigan, his former employer, declined to comment.

Canada's Industry Minister Melanie Joly said on Thursday that the government was "very glad that these fantastic professors are coming".

Asked whether the new government programme was poaching US talent and could be viewed by the Trump administration as an escalation of the US-Canada trade war, she said on Thursday: "The US administration is taking its own decisions and we're taking ours."

Some of the researchers chosen for the programme, like Guikema, were born and raised in the US. Others are Canadians who worked abroad and are now returning home.

Peter Caravan, who for two decades worked as a biopharmaceutical researcher and professor at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School, appeared emotional at a news conference announcing the research appointments on Thursday.

Caravan is researching how illnesses like cancers and chronic diseases can be better detected - work that will now be done out of the University of British Columbia in Vancouver.

Steven Lamy, a professor of International Relations at the University of Southern California, argued that major grant agencies had "been cut and politicised" by the current US administration.

"All of a sudden employment offers from external universities are attractive," he said.

Stephanie Burt, an English professor at Harvard University, believed the funding cuts were "a generational disaster for science and scientists".

She told the BBC that Canada had offered a "far more welcoming environment" for academics.

US universities are still among the top ranked in the world, according to QS Universities Rankings, with the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Stanford and Harvard in the top five.

Lynn Pasquerella, the president of the American Association of Colleges and Universities, said institutions felt "helpless" in the face of federal and state cuts.

The deeper concern, she added, was "not the short-term brain drain" but "the possibility that the US could become less attractive as a place to pursue knowledge".

Canada's retaliation tests the limit of American power under Trump

items.title: Berlin is being blackmailed by hackers, mayor says
items.summary: Kai Wegner says the German capital and city-state would not cave in to a ransom demand for data stolen in a cyber-attack.
items.content:
Berlin is being blackmailed by hackers who were able to compromise city systems and steal data earlier this month, its mayor has said.

Kai Wegner said officials would not cave in to the ransom demand, which came on Thursday evening. He did not say how much was being sought, though Der Spiegel reports the hackers are demanding 30 bitcoin, worth around €2m (£1.7m).

Some of the German capital's online systems were forced to close down as a result of the attack, while investigators were working to understand what data had been taken.

The Rhysida group, which is thought to operate from Russia and eastern Europe, and was behind a previous attack on the British Museum, has reportedly taken responsibility.

It has said on its website it intends to begin auctioning the 5.79 terabytes of data it was able to steal from Berlin in seven days' time, according to news agency Reuters.

He said state police, prosecutors and federal security services were working to investigate the suspected perpetrators "with the utmost urgency", adding that inquiries into the "content and scope of the compromised data are being pursued with great intensity".

Officials for the city-state said an initial data leak occurred between 7 and 12 August.

Then, on 14 August, two department networks were shut down, making applications for housing benefits and payments impossible for several days.

Forensic investigations had since revealed further data leaks within Berlin's transport and environment department, officials said.

"It cannot be ruled out that personal or other non-public data may also be affected," the mayor's office said in a statement on Friday.

Authorities in the capital have not named the suspected cyber-attackers, though Der Spiegel is carrying a screenshot of the Rhysida group's dark web site claiming to possess files including contracts, non-disclosure agreements, personnel files, passwords and thousands of personal contact details.

It is also displaying a countdown, after which it says it will begin auctioning off the data with a starting price of 30 bitcoin - the same amount of the cryptocurrency being sought from Berlin, the German newspaper reports.

The Rhysida group has claimed hundreds of attacks since it emerged in 2023, studies say, and the group has targeted government insititutions and businesses of varying sizes in numerous countries.

It successfully infiltrated the British Museum's computer systems in 2023, disrupting services and stealing around 500,000 files.

When the UK institution refused to pay the ransom, the group published the files - containing the personal data of visitors, subscribers and staff - on the dark web.

The Berlin cyber-attack comes roughly a month before the city holds elections, though state senator Iris Spranger insisted that election infrastructure had not been compromised.

items.title: 97-year-old woman rescued after Nepali floods looked like 'a warrior'
items.summary: A 97-year-old woman, Guna Maya Bohara, survived the flash floods and was rescued using an excavator.
items.content:
A 97-year-old woman pulled from flood debris in Nepal is recovering in hospital, according to her doctors.

Guna Maya Bohara's great-nephew, Dipak Bohara, has told BBC Nepali she looked like "a warrior" who had returned victorious from battle.

The operation to pull Bohara out of the rubble of her care home took four hours.

Bohara travelled from Kathmandu to help rescue his great-aunt.

Hundreds of people have been confirmed dead after Wednesday's flash floods, which scientists believe were triggered by a glacier collapsing in the Himalayan border region with Tibet.

Video produced by Mansi Kapur and Kamal Pariyar. Video edited by Suneth Perera, Jasmin Dyer and Andrew Webb.

items.title: Greenland says findings on genocide allegation not final
items.summary: Experts examined the use of forced contraception on the Inuit community during the 1960s and 70s.
items.content:
Greenland's justice minister has said the government cannot conclude whether genocide was committed against the Inuit community after experts examined the use of forced contraception in the 1960s and 70s.

"We cannot say, on behalf of the government, whether there was genocide," Marianne Paviasen told reporters. "This is something we can continue to debate."

Two reports on the practice were released on Friday, a year after Denmark apologised for the treatment of Inuit women and girls in its autonomous territory.

Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said a "reconciliation commission" would be set up while Danish PM Mette Frederiksen promised the governments would work together.

Denmark has passed a compensation law to pay 300,000 Danish crowns (£34,404; $46,800) to each woman affected by the policy.

Records from the national archives show that, between 1966 and 1970, 4,500 Greenlandic women and girls, some as young as 13, had an intra-uterine device (IUD) implanted under a birth-control programme administered by Danish doctors.

In recent years, many women came forward to say they had been fitted with an IUD without their knowledge or consent.

Use of the birth control was so widespread that Greenland's population growth severely slowed.

Frederiksen issued an apology last August to Greenlandic women and their families affected by "systematic discrimination".

In 2024, a former prime minister of Greenland, Mute B Egede, described the practice as "genocide".

Under the UN Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide , external , one definition of genocide is "imposing measures intended to prevent births" within a "national, ethnical, racial or religious group".

The territory tasked a panel of four experts with establishing whether human rights had been violated and whether such violations met the definition of genocide.

However, the panel split, with two members resigning and producing a separate report.

The two experts who remained, Alaskan lawyer Dalee Sambo Dorough and University of Copenhagen law professor Miriam Cullen, found in their report that the rights of Inuit women in Greenland had been violated.

But they said that they could not conclude that genocide had taken place "on the basis of contraceptive practices alone".

They added that genocidal intent by Denmark remained a "possible inference" that a court might establish, based on evidence that fell outside the scope of their report, such as the removal of Inuit children to be raised by Danish families.

The rival report, produced by Jonas Christoffersen, former head of the Danish Institute for Human Rights, and Jensine Nedergaard, a psychologist who had worked in Greenland, accepted that women had been wronged but could not establish the extent of their mistreatment.

They found no evidence "any authority or health professional at any time had any intention of destroying the Greenlandic population".

Reacting on Friday, Greenland's justice minister said the two reports were so different that one "says there was no genocide at all" while the other "says there could have been".

Greenland contraception scandal victims hear Danish PM's emotional apology

Denmark apologises to Greenland's forced contraception victims

One woman affected by the forced contraception policy, Henriette Berthelsen, told news agency AFP before the reports were presented that their conclusions had been skewed from the start because no Greenlandic Inuits had been appointed as experts.

"For me, this is not just about history or politics. It's my body, my life and my right to self-determination," she said.

"And once again, I see that it is others who will investigate and define what was done to me and to other Inuit women."

Another woman, Inger Platou, 70, told Reuters that she remembered waking up from what she had been told was a minor operation to discover an IUD had been inserted without her consent.

"It turns out we were treated like animals," she said. "Without consent, they just wanted to stop women from giving birth or having children. It was a very inhumane act."

A doctor, she added, later told her complications from the coil had left her unable to become pregnant. She went on to adopt two children from Colombia.

"We are very deferential to authority because we are colonial children," she said.

Reacting to the reports on Friday, Frederiksen said: "We will handle the political process together with the government of Greenland. The most important thing for me is that we find the right path together."

Greenland was a Danish colony until 1953 and did not gain home rule until 1979. Copenhagen continued to oversee its healthcare system until 1992.

The Inuit, or mixed Danish and Inuit, make up nearly 90% of the island's population of 56,000.

The birth-control campaign was designed to control the territory's population, which had ballooned since the 1950s, aided by modernisation and better healthcare. This growth, in addition to an increasing rate of teenage pregnancies, had alarmed the Danish authorities.

In 1970, the campaign was considered a "success" as fertility rates had fallen sharply, though the rate continued to fall for some time after that. In the eight years from the campaign's inception in 1966 until 1974 when it levelled off, Greenland's fertility rate plunged from seven children per woman to 2.3.

items.title: Russia ramps up rhetoric but wants to avoid war with Nato, Western officials say
items.summary: But they say Moscow will likely continue its "hybrid activity" against Nato members, short of direct military action.
items.content:
Russian President Vladimir Putin wants to avoid a direct military confrontation with Nato, despite increasingly hostile rhetoric aimed at the UK and other allies over their support for Ukraine, Western officials believe.

Some reports have suggested the visit by CIA chief John Radcliffe to Moscow this week was, in part, to warn Russia against a possible attack on a member of the Euro-Atlantic military alliance.

But the Western officials, who asked not to be named, said recent warnings from Moscow, including that UK forces could be targeted in future or that its weapons factories could be hit, were "nothing new".

They were, they suggested, consistent with Russia's military doctrine to apply pressure on the West.

The officials suggested that the hostile rhetoric was also a reflection of the growing pressure Putin is facing at home, with slow and costly gains in Ukraine along with the impact of Ukrainian long-range strikes deep inside Russia.

Putin and his officials have repeatedly dismissed warnings of Russian plans to attack Nato countries as hysteria. And US President Donald Trump appears to believe the Russian leader – saying this week that "he's not going to attack a Nato territory".

Not long before launching his full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Putin had given public assurances that he had no intention of attacking Russia's neighbour - despite overwhelming US intelligence that such preparations were in full swing.

However, the senior Western officials said on Friday that Russia would likely continue its "hybrid activity", short of direct military action, using methods such as cyber-attacks, sabotage and even assassination attempts.

They said that was aimed at breaking Western resolve and support for Ukraine. One official highlighted the risks of that Russian strategy leading to a miscalculation -which could spark a military confrontation.

Russia is suspected of being behind a string of recent drone incidents in several Nato countries.

Earlier this month, a drone loaded with explosives reached a runway in Germany's Leipzig airport - a key logistics hub for transferring military equipment to Ukraine. There is no proof to link the incident directly to Russia, which has denied any role.

It came amid a string of drone sightings over European airports and military bases that began last year and which are also suspected of being the work of Russia, though it again denies this.

Following the Leipzig incident, the head of France's security services warned that "we must consider the possibility of direct, more violent hostile actions on our national soil".

Still, one Western official said Nato allies should remain calm but not complacent. The UK government has already made clear that recent Russian threats will not deter its support for Ukraine.

The Western officials said the Ukraine war had "escalated" this year, with both Moscow and Kyiv stepping up their own long-range strike campaigns.

Putin, they said, had not changed his maximalist objectives, despite some signs of increasing frustrations back home.

They said petrol shortages in Russia were having an impact on support for the war. They believed there was increasing political pressure on the Russian leader, but that this did not pose a critical challenge to his power.

Russia is still making slow gains in the eastern Donbas region. But it's also facing heavy casualties.

The officials said Russia was losing 6,000 more soldiers a month - either killed or wounded - than it can recruit.

That said, there is no indication yet that the Kremlin leader will resort to mass mobilisation.

items.title: Satellite images reveal scale of flood devastation in Nepal villages
items.summary: Before-and-after images show villages, bridges and a key Nepal-Tibet border crossing washed away by devastating floodwaters.
items.content:
New satellite imagery has revealed the scale of the devastation along Nepal's Trishuli River caused by Wednesday's deadly flash flood, triggered by a glacier collapse.

Before-and-after images show how sections of the valley, where a torrent of floodwater and debris surged through, destroyed villages, bridges and hydroelectric power stations.

Hundreds of people have been killed and thousands more are missing, Nepalese officials say.

Among the worst-hit locations reviewed by BBC Verify was a key Nepal-Tibet border crossing, which was engulfed by a rush of floodwater and captured on camera.

The satellite imagery from US-based intelligence firm Vantor, shows the site has been almost entirely washed away. Shocking CCTV footage showed the moment as the deluge of water swept over buildings as people tried to escape.

Damage and mud can be seen more than 2.5km (1.5 miles) upstream, reaching 100m (330 ft) above the area it first hit.

A few miles further south is the village of Timure, which has now largely disappeared.

The walls of the valley at this point are steep, reaching up to 50m above the water line. The image shows most of the houses perched on this slope are now gone or covered in mud.

A further 10km (eight miles) downstream, where the Trishuli River winds through Syapru Besi, satellite imagery now shows the village covered by mud, rock and other debris. Houses and other structures have disappeared, including bridges and a hydroelectric power station.

One of the larger villages to be struck by the full force of the flood was Trishuli, where some of the earliest verified footage of the disaster emerged from.

A satellite image of the town and surrounding agricultural land, which is about 45km (28 miles) downstream from the border, show an entire neighbourhood has been essentially washed away.

Verified videos of the town show a bridge collapsing as the river surges forward. At the very same moment from ground level, footage filmed from inside a bus shows people crying out in distress and trying to flee as they see the water rushing down the river.

Other dramatic videos show people sheltering inside a house, peering over the edge of a balcony as they watch a torrent of floodwater wash away almost everything around them, knocking large metal debris and a vehicle toward the building.

Somehow the house remains intact and survivors can be seen in a second verified video standing surrounded by mud once the floodwater had receded.

Imagery from satellite provider Planet Labs released today has also provided a clearer view of the disaster's origins at the collapsed glacier, the moment of which has been captured on a verified drone video.

The satellite image shows an enormous chunk of the glacier has fallen away, carving an enormous path of rock and debris where water rushed through the valley.

At the base of the landslide, trees and other vegetation have been stripped at a height of more than 300m above the riverbed.

This destructive path continues westwards along with the swelled river, before heading southwards.

Satellite images also show the formation of a barrier lake at the base of the landslide's path, which Chinese authorities have warned poses a major risk of further flooding and has hampered rescue efforts.

Dr Argha Banerjee, a glaciologist at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, told BBC Verify that it was not possible determine from the images how stable the barrier was or how likely the lake was to drain suddenly.

But he said there was no significant increase in its surface area between Wednesday and Thursday, despite water continuing to flow into the lake.

Dr Banerjee said there was a visible drainage channel, which suggests some water was already escaping downstream, adding that the its volume was "not alarmingly large" and appeared to have stabilised.

The extent of the damage on the Tibetan side of the border remains unclear. It is a strictly controlled region which China annexed in the 1950s, where foreign media access is heavily restricted. BBC Verify has so far been unable find verifiable footage from the area.

The satellite imagery - which only provides an initial glimpse into the damage of the flood - has been published by Vantor as part of its Open Data Program to help aid authorities establish where best to focus their efforts to locate the missing, rescue survivors and recover the dead.

Additional reporting Shruti Menon, Merlyn Thomas and Alex Murray. Graphics by Mesut Ersoz and Mike Hill.

'High risk' of lake breaching and causing second flood, warns China

'Our parents were crossing the border an hour before the flood hit'

items.title: Mykhailo Fedorov, l’ex ministro della Difesa ucraino rimosso da Zelensky, sarà consulente per l’innovazione del ministro Crosetto
items.content:
Il ministro della Difesa italiano, Guido Crosetto, ha annunciato di avere nominato come consulente per l’innovazione Mykhailo Fedorov, l’ex ministro della Difesa ucraino che a luglio era stato rimosso dal presidente Volodymyr Zelensky.

Crosetto, che venerdì ha ricevuto Fedorov a Roma, ha citato l’esperienza e i successi dell’Ucraina nella guerra con i droni , oltre al lavoro di Fedorov nella digitalizzazione dell’apparato statale ucraino, che aveva contribuito a renderlo un ministro molto apprezzato, soprattutto dai giovani. Fedorov ha confermato la nomina, dicendo: «Aiuterò l’Italia ad adattarsi alle tecnologie belliche moderne, a rafforzare il suo settore della Difesa e ad adattarsi alle nascenti sfide alla sicurezza globale». Ha presentato l’incontro come tappa di un viaggio internazionale, in cui potrebbero essere decise nomine simili.

Dopo il licenziamento di Fedorov, avvenuto a causa di uno scontro con i comandi delle forze armate su come dovesse essere impostata la strategia di guerra, in Ucraina c’erano state manifestazioni per chiedere il suo reintegro. Zelensky era andato incontro ai manifestanti rimuovendo il comandante delle forze armate Oleksandr Syrsky , con cui Fedorov si era scontrato, e offrendo a Fedorov di tornare al governo con una nuova carica. Fedorov aveva rifiutato e la settimana scorsa ha chiesto nuove elezioni , che sono vietate dalla legge marziale e poco realistiche da organizzare con la guerra in corso. Così si è posizionato come un rivale di Zelensky, ma ha probabilmente sprecato un’occasione politica , facendo una richiesta impopolare che ha allontanato i suoi sostenitori.

items.title: Cos’ha detto Sigfrido Ranucci sulla sua rimozione da “Report”
items.summary: Secondo lui i due giornalisti scelti dalla Rai per sostituirlo «mortificano le professionalità» del programma
items.content:
Il giornalista Sigfrido Ranucci, che la Rai ha rimosso dalla conduzione di Report , ha commentato in modo molto duro e sprezzante la nomina dei suoi sostituti, i giornalisti investigativi Giulia Presutti e Daniele Piervincenzi: «Al mio posto sono state scelte due persone che mortificano le professionalità che per 30 anni hanno fatto la storia di Report e del servizio pubblico», ha scritto in un post .

Contro la nomina di Piervincenzi e Presutti, collega di Ranucci che lavora a Report dal 2018, si erano già espressi con toni simili gli stessi inviati del programma, che in una nota avevano definito la scelta dei due «completamente irricevibile» e avevano aggiunto di non ritenerli «in alcun modo rappresentativi della storia e dei valori di Report », arrivando anche a minacciare di andarsene in blocco dalla redazione del programma nel caso in cui la Rai non ritrattasse la decisione.

Per Report Presutti si è occupata soprattutto di politica, sanità e note vicende giudiziarie; Piervincenzi invece non ha mai lavorato a Report ma è alla Rai dal 2016 e sempre in programmi di approfondimento e inchiesta.

Nello stesso post Ranucci ha detto in modo molto enfatico che dopo questa vicenda è intenzionato a condurre «la battaglia più importante della sua vita per la libertà di stampa, lo farò per i miei e per i vostri figli». E poi: «Mi rifiuto di lasciare alle future generazioni questo mondo mostruoso, governato da persone mostruose e vigliacche che non tollerano il giornalismo libero e i magistrati indipendenti».

In queste settimane in cui si è parlato molto di lui e dell’inchiesta giudiziaria sull’attentato nei suoi confronti , Ranucci ha assunto spesso un atteggiamento molto vittimista. Ha detto di essere il bersaglio di una campagna ostile del governo e si è paragonato a importanti personaggi della storia italiana vittime di attentati di mafia, come i magistrati Giovanni Falcone e Paolo Borsellino.

La decisione della Rai di rimuoverlo ha a che fare proprio con l’inchiesta, in cui si è scoperto che l’attentato era stato organizzato da Valter Lavitola , imprenditore coinvolto in diversi scandali della politica italiana degli ultimi vent’anni e molto amico di Ranucci. Secondo la procura di Roma, che sta indagando sul caso, Lavitola avrebbe pianificato l’attentato per accrescere la popolarità di Ranucci e spingerlo poi a entrare in politica.

Ranucci non è indagato e secondo la procura non era a conoscenza del piano di Lavitola, ma a partire dall’inchiesta è emersa una consuetudine tra i due che molti hanno giudicato eccessiva e compromettente per un giornalista dell’importanza di Ranucci, di cui Lavitola era sia fonte che confidente intimo. I rapporti tra Ranucci e la dirigenza della Rai in ogni caso si erano deteriorati da tempo.

In queste settimane Ranucci aveva più volte suggerito che la maggioranza stesse solo cercando un pretesto per censurarlo, visto che Report ha spesso fatto inchieste su politici di destra e al governo. Diversi esponenti dei partiti di destra al governo in queste settimane avevano chiesto la sua rimozione o sospensione.

items.title: Thieves steal 600-diamond necklace from Vienna museum in broad daylight
items.summary: Police are hunting two suspects they believe bought a ticket for the exhibition to get at the jewellery.
items.content:
An international manhunt is under way for two men who stole a necklace decorated with more than 600 diamonds from a museum in Vienna after buying a ticket for the exhibition in which it was being displayed.

Police said the two suspects smashed a glass display case at the Vienna Museum of Applied Arts (MAK) on Thursday afternoon and grabbed the platinum and diamond necklace, which is believed to be worth more than $4m (£3m; €3.5m).

The necklace, which was designed for the former Egyptian royal family, was part of an exhibition on the jewellers Van Cleef & Arpels, due to run at MAK until September.

The theft is the latest in a series of spectacular heists of artefacts at European museums.

Vienna police released photos of the two suspects, who were unmasked, captured on security cameras. They are appealing for the public to come forward with information.

The police said in a statement that one of the perpetrators was also believed to have been carrying what was thought to be a real firearm.

After seizing the necklace, they fled "towards the Vienna Stadtpark" just south of the museum, they said.

Lilli Hollein, MAK general director, said "the theft of a highly valuable piece of jewellery... has hit us hard".

She said in a statement that MAK had developed a security plan with Van Cleef & Arpels specifically for the exhibition, adding: "Security issues were taken very seriously and all security measures were carefully prepared."

Hollein said staff had reacted calmly and followed the established procedures when the "armed incident" occurred, and that no one had been injured.

She added that MAK had thoroughly reviewed its security measures ahead of the exhibition, "particularly in light of the incidents at major museums in recent years".

Also on Thursday was one of the most important troves of prehistoric jewellery and artefacts was stolen from a Spanish museum.

Four Renaissance paintings were stolen from a museum in Sicily earlier this month, while three paintings by Renoir, Cézanne and Matisse worth millions of euros were taken from a museum in Parma earlier in the year.

These heists came after the brazen daylight raid on the Louvre in Paris, in which a masked gang stole priceless jewels last October.

The string of thefts have raised questions about the security of European cultural institutions.

Europol said museum thefts were "becoming increasingly aggressive, with a shift towards violent and forceful methods", adding this "may indicate the involvement of new criminal networks".

The necklace stolen in Vienna on Friday was designed for the former Egyptian royal family and was worn by Queen Nazli in 1939 for the marriage of her daughter Fawzia to the future Shah of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi.

Van Cleef & Arpels describes it as a "triumph of white jewellery". The diamonds on the necklace weigh in excess of 200 carats.

When it was auctioned a decade ago, it had an estimated worth of $3.6m-$4.6m.

Police dog units have been deployed in Vienna and the province of Lower Austria, while forensic experts are analysing evidence and CCTV footage.

items.title: Pixel 11 Pro XL, recensione. Born for the USA
items.summary: Chi si disinteressa totalmente della scheda tecnica e vuole solo uno smartphone che funziona bene lo amerà, chi guarda all'hardware lo vedrà come uno scandalo. Perché i problemi ci sono, e non sono pochi. Il Pixel come sempre divide, ma bisogna anche capire che per Google fare smartphone è più difficile che per ogni altra azienda. ... Leggi tutto
items.content:
Per questa recensione avevamo in mente due titoli. " Born for the USA ", perché vedremo che alla fine è uno smartphone studiato e pensato per conquistare quella fetta di pubblico americano che cerca un'alternativa ad Apple, ma incentrata sui servizi di Mountain View, e " Il capolavoro di Google ", che era un titolo provocatorio ma azzeccato, perché crediamo il Pixel sia davvero lo smartphone che Google voleva fare in questo momento particolare. Ovvero uno smartphone che a d un pubblico per nulla attento alle specifiche sembrerà comunque un ottimo prodotto, al netto di qualche difetto risolvibile via software, ma che al tempo stesso sia economico da produrre.

Questa sarà quindi al tempo stesso una recensione e una spiegazione del perché il Pixel 11 Pro è uscito così: Google non ha sbagliato, e non è certo incapace di fare telefoni come pensano in molti.

Google ha risparmiato, ed è probabilmente una delle poche aziende produttrici che guadagna vendendo questo smartphone, e nel farlo ha anche messo in pista il prodotto commercialmente più vicino alla sua strategia aziendale, ovvero fare in modo che nel mondo del mobile l'IA passi per il cloud (quello di Google, ovvio), disinnescando sul nascere un ecosistema Android cross-vendor che possa far partire decollare l'uso dell'IA in locale.

Alla fine, tra i due titoli, abbiamo scelto il primo, perché siamo davvero convinti che se abitassimo a New York, con un potere di acquisto superiore a quello europeo e con tutte le funzioni che gli utenti americani hanno (e noi europei no), di questo Pixel daremmo un giudizio diverso.

Il Pixel è progettato guardando al mercato americano, dove troviamo una base di utenti Apple enorme e una quota di utenti Samsung importante; c'è poi Motorola, staccata di molto, che vende quasi esclusivamente smartphone di fascia bassa.

Inutile sottolineare l'assenza praticamente totale dei brand cinesi consumer: Xiaomi, Huawei, Oppo, vivo e Honor non esistono, OnePlus ci ha provato e ha fallito.

Google è quindi l'unica alternativa americana all'iPhone, ed è un'alternativa che piace: sta raggiungendo Motorola al terzo posto, anche se si tratta di numeri ancora piccolissimi.

Per questo crediamo che ogni considerazione che viene fatta sul Pixel vada vista con un occhio da telefono per gli Usa. Ha la batteria piccola e non usa il silicio-carbonio? C'è un motivo: la batteria del Pro XL, 5.115 mAh, è di fatto la più capiente che si possa montare mantenendo una singola cella al litio, perché in Usa oltre una certa soglia di wattora per cella, 20 Wh, scattano requisiti più stringenti per il trasporto . Con una batteria da 5.500 mAh il Pixel sarebbe invendibile negli Stati Uniti: andrebbero previsti trasporti speciali. Certo, si possono usare due celle, ma diventa decisamente più complesso da produrre, da gestire (per il bilanciamento) e più costoso. Insomma, certe scelte sono obbligate.

Intanto che ci siamo, prima di passare alla recensione vera e propria, introduciamo anche il secondo tema, quello del risparmio: Google è un'azienda enorme, al cui interno ogni divisione guarda al proprio orticello. La divisione che si occupa di Android, quella che stringe le partnership con i vari produttori di telefoni, che gestisce i profitti dello store e di tutto quello che gira attorno all'ecosistema Google, non ha niente a che fare con quella che produce l'hardware. La divisione "devices", che progetta i Pixel, i Pixel Watch e gli altri dispositivi, come le altre deve dimostrare di saper sopravvivere da sola, un po' come Xbox dentro Microsoft: deve realizzare un prodotto con un margine di guadagno soddisfacente .

Google, con i Pixel, è probabilmente l'azienda più svantaggiata rispetto a ogni altra azienda che oggi che produce smartphone Android. Non solo in Europa deve competere con i produttori cinesi, che arrivano sul mercato extra Cina con hardware super pompato a prezzi che solo una filiera integrata e sostenuta a livello di sistema (e anche dal Governo) riesce a tenere bassi, ma mentre tutti gli altri produttori ricevono incentivi da Google, grazie ad accordi di revenue sharing legati all'adozione di Android, alla search e alla preinstallazione dei servizi, lei quegli incentivi non li riceve . Google non paga sé stessa.

Ci troviamo in un momento terribile: aumentano i prezzi delle memorie, aumentano i prezzi di TSMC e dei wafer, aumenta tutto, e a Google non resta che fare una cosa: risparmiare il più possibile realizzando un prodotto che sembri comunque ottimo . Lo ha fatto evitando di comprare il SoC da terzi, il che significa non pagare a Qualcomm centinaia di dollari per uno Snapdragon, lo ha fatto spendendo meno per le licenze (PowerVR, Mali è troppo costosa) e risparmiando il più possibile su RAM, storage e sul suo stesso processore, il Tensor G6. Che è stato privato di tutto quello che non serve a un utente base.

Sulla costruzione c'è poco da eccepire. Il telefono è fatto bene ed è assemblato bene: Google su questo fronte ha sbagliato più volte in passato, l'anno scorso un esemplare aveva il vetro non perfettamente a filo con la cornice, ma l'unità in prova è perfetta. Le dimensioni sono praticamente quelle del Pixel 10 Pro XL (162,7 × 76,5 × 8,5 mm contro 162,8 × 76,6 × 8,5 mm), mentre il peso scende di poco, a 226 grammi. Resta comunque uno smartphone pesante.

La nostra versione è quella totalmente satinata: cornice nera opaca, retro nero opaco che non trattiene alcuna impronta e Camera Bar anch'essa nera, ridisegnata, più sottile e con un vetro continuo a protezione delle lenti.

Attenzione a questa finitura: la scocca è anodizzata, ma il colore è solo superficiale e una caduta (sigh, ci è successo) basta a scoprire il tenero alluminio; la Camera Bar, con il suo profilo vivo, perde colore dopo una settimana. L'abbiamo usato senza cover, tenendolo in tasca, e il bordo della Camera Bar, a 90° perfetti e quasi tagliente, sta perdendo il nero in alcuni punti. Dalla foto sotto si può vedere.

Non mancano la certificazione IP68 e un rivestimento del vetro frontale in Gorilla Glass Victus 2 che secondo Google è due volte più resistente ai graffi rispetto al Pixel 10 Pro. Effettivamente il vetro, anche se lo abbiamo tenuto in tasca senza pellicola, è praticamente perfetto.

Il display è ottimo: un Super Actua OLED LTPO da 6,8 pollici, 2992 × 1344 pixel per 486 ppi, refresh variabile da 1 a 120 Hz. La luminosità di picco sale a 3.600 nit, con contenuti HDR che toccano i 2.400 nit e un rapporto di contrasto dichiarato oltre 2.000.000:1.

Sotto il sole diretto il pannello resta perfettamente leggibile e ci mette un po' ad entrare in protezione, e forse la sua qualità migliore è il modo in cui visualizza le foto e la preview fotografica.

Non sappiamo perché, ma di fianco a OPPO Find X9 Pro e a Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra, quando si scatta con il Pixel, l'anteprima a schermo ha una qualità nettamente migliore , e la stessa cosa accade per la visione delle foto dopo lo scatto: sarà la gestione dell'HDR, o del tone mapping, ma ogni foto scattata dal Pixel sembra più bella vista sul suo schermo. Anche se sulla carta resta un pannello a 8 bit che ottiene i 10 bit tramite dithering, la qualità dello schermo è davvero eccellente.

Sotto la scocca in alluminio e vetro, oltre ai magneti del Pixel Snap, quest'anno c'è una nuova vapor chamber, e l'effetto è lo stesso che avevamo osservato su iPhone 17 Pro: una quantità maggiore di calore viene trasportata verso l'esterno, con la scocca che diventa un grande dissipatore.

Chi arriva da un Pixel di generazione precedente avrà l'impressione che questo Pixel 11 Pro sia più caldo in molte situazioni , ma non è un difetto: sposta il calore verso l'esterno invece di accumularlo internamente, ed è per questo che lo schermo ci mette qualche minuto in più per entrare in protezione.

Il Tensor G6 non è il chip a 2 nm di cui si è parlato per settimane, lo avevamo già detto. È prodotto da TSMC con processo N3P e, sebbene sia un 3 nm migliorato, è sempre la stessa classe di nodo del Tensor G5 dell'anno scorso. L'N3P rispetto all'N3E porta a qualche miglioria, ma poco importa, perché è evidente che l'ultima cosa a cui ha pensato Google è stata fare un processore che potesse competere con MediaTek o Snapdragon. Non serviva: loro devono dimostrare potenza per vendere ai produttori che hanno bisogno di un chip, Google doveva realizzare il prodotto più adatto alle sue esigenze e in linea con i suoi costi.

Per quanto i benchmark, se guardiamo al risultato finale, facciano vedere una differenza abissale tra uno Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen5 e il Tensor G6 è bene andare un po' più nel dettaglio, e vedere cosa ci dicono davvero i numeri. Perché i benchmark, lo abbiamo sempre detto, se vengono presi fuori da un contesto servono davvero a poco .

Prendiamo Geekbench 7, che è forse il più noto ed è anche quello che più ricalca le metodologie di test di SPEC, il riferimento del settore. Geekbench 7 fa eseguire allo smartphone una sequenza di operazioni prestabilite, l'apertura di un PDF, la compressione di un archivio, un tipo specifico di calcolo, assegnando a ognuna un punteggio; questi punteggi, sommati, danno poi il totale.

items.title: Violence breaks out in Ceuta as migrant crisis continues
items.summary: A group of migrants is accused of throwing stones at a military vehicle, while some locals set fire to their camps on the beach.
items.content:
A month after tens of thousands of migrants entered the city of Ceuta, a Spanish exclave in North Africa, there have been outbreaks of violence as tensions mount between locals and foreign arrivals.

The Spanish government has been accused by opposition parties of struggling to manage the crisis effectively.

Ceuta's residents have complained of feeling unsafe on the streets, as well as expressing concerns about the burden being placed on public services.

At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July. Most swam around a border fence and at least 100 people died during the mass crossing, according to figures from Ceuta's mayor.

The vast majority of the migrants returned to Morocco within hours of their arrival, but several thousand remain in Ceuta, many of them children, and most are sleeping rough on beaches or streets.

Anti-migrant demonstrations earlier this month were largely peaceful, but in recent days they have become increasingly violent.

On Thursday, several dozen locals prevented Red Cross personnel from distributing food and water to the migrants. Afterwards, some set fire to migrant camps on Trampolín beach, the main site where they have been sleeping, and there were also clashes with the police.

Those incidents came hours after the arrest of 12 migrants who were accused of throwing stones at a military vehicle, breaking its windows and injuring the four men inside. That same morning there were reports of vigilante groups pursuing migrants through the streets.

Journalists and film crews have also reported being threatened.

"This is a city which has been under pressure, […] which has the right to normality," the mayor of the exclave, the conservative Juan Jesús Vivas, told Antena 3 television.

"The dignity of Spain is a stake right now in Ceuta," he said.

The socialist-led government of Pedro Sánchez has appealed for calm and accused Vivas's People's Party (PP) and the far-right Vox of stoking the tensions.

José María Figaredo, a member of Congress for Vox, is being investigated for a possible hate crime after saying, soon after the migrants' arrival, that they should be "hunted down, one by one".

Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska told a congressional committee: "We have heard during these weeks rhetoric and comments that contribute to the stigmatisation of immigrants and which feed social division at a moment when what we need is responsibility and statesmanship."

Javier Celaya, who represents Ceuta in Congress for the PP, accused the government of treating "the invaders as victims when the real victims are us, the people of Ceuta".

On Friday, all the parties in the Ceuta local assembly signed a declaration condemning violence.

Earlier this week, the government centralised management of the situation, overriding the local authority, after criticism that it had been slow to respond.

Defence Minister Margarita Robles also apologised to those in Ceuta who "may have felt, or who even still feel, abandoned or not sufficiently cared", as the government unveiled plans to overhaul the country's immigration laws.

Much of the recent ill-feeling in the city appears to be driven by government plans to move migrants into existing public buildings, such as sports centres, in order to be able to process their legal status in an orderly way and return those not eligible for asylum to Morocco.

Many local people, and Vivas, oppose this initiative, due to concerns that it will move the migrants closer to residential areas.

The government is also facing questions about who was behind the mass migrant crossing.

Politicians on the right and the far left have accused Morocco of involvement, pointing to its alleged use of the border with Spain in the past to exert political pressure.

Sánchez and his Socialist Party instead blame people traffickers, insisting that Rabat is a reliable partner which facilitated the immediate return of most of the arrivals.

Nonetheless, the crisis has placed the sovereignty of Ceuta, and its fellow autonomous city Melilla, under the spotlight.

Morocco has maintained a longstanding claim to the territories, which it has reiterated in recent weeks.

Spain's Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares said he "roundly rejected" such comments by Morocco.

"I don't speak about, nor have I spoken about, nor are we going to speak about Spain's territorial integrity with Morocco or with anyone else," he told the congressional committee.

items.title: A Cremona un violento temporale ha fatto gravi danni
items.summary: Vento e grandine hanno divelto alberi, coperture di capannoni e pezzi di tetti, distrutto una guglia della cattedrale e danneggiato il palazzo comunale
items.content:
Venerdì pomeriggio, poco dopo le 16, a Cremona c’è stato un breve ma violento temporale che ha causato molti e gravi danni. Il forte vento, combinato alla grandine, ha fatto cadere alberi e danneggiato edifici: tetti di abitazioni , anzitutto, ma anche coperture di capannoni. Ha pure distrutto parti di edifici storici: è crollata la copertura della torre civica della sede del comune, è stata distrutta una guglia della cattedrale e un’altra decina di chiese risulta danneggia.

Non è chiaro se ci siano persone ferite, e quante: il sito di notizie locale Cremona Oggi scrive che che ce ne sono 41, diverse delle quali sarebbero rimaste incastrate in automobili su cui erano cadute piante e alberi. I feriti sono stati soccorsi e stanno ricevendo cure; non ci sono notizie di feriti gravi né di morti. Almeno otto famiglie hanno dovuto lasciare le loro case.

Vari alberi sono caduti sulle automobili, distruggendole, o sulle strade, bloccandole: molte sono state chiuse al traffico ed è stata sospesa la circolazione dei treni nella stazione. Circa 10mila auto sono state danneggiate.

Nella zona della fiera di Cremona è saltata la copertura in alluminio di un padiglione, che è precipitata in un parcheggio accartocciandosi. Sempre a causa del vento sono stati abbattuti cartelli e ribaltate transenne.

items.title: La Piramide di Caio Cestio a Roma riaprirà dopo 3 anni di restauri
items.content:
Giovedì la Soprintendenza speciale di Roma ha annunciato che la Piramide di Caio Cestio riaprirà al pubblico dal 4 settembre. La Piramide è un monumento molto riconoscibile risalente all’epoca romana che si trova a sud del centro storico di Roma, nel quartiere Ostiense. Si potrà visitare solo su prenotazione tramite visite guidate gratuite della durata di circa 45 minuti, e sono programmate per ora fino al 31 ottobre. Non è chiaro se verranno organizzate altre visite successivamente.

Negli ultimi tre anni la Piramide è stata chiusa al pubblico per alcuni lavori di restauro finanziati con il PNRR. Il risultato più significativo è stato la realizzazione del nuovo sistema di illuminazione interna ed esterna. Sono stati migliorati anche l’accessibilità del monumento, il giardino che lo circonda e i pannelli informativi.

La Piramide è alta più di 36 metri e ha una base quadrata con un lato lungo quasi 30 metri. Fu realizzata come tomba di Caio Cestio, un importante uomo politico romano, tra il 18 e il 12 avanti Cristo. Dopo che gli antichi Romani avevano conquistato l’Egitto, pochi anni prima, a Roma andava di moda costruire edifici funebri ispirati a quelli egiziani: questa piramide è l’unico che si è conservato fino a oggi.

Le visite serali saranno tutti i venerdì di settembre alle 19, alle 20 e alle 21 (sono prenotabili qua ), mentre le visite di giorno saranno tutti i sabati di settembre e ottobre (tranne il 26 settembre) alle 16:30, alle 17:30 e alle 18:30 (sono prenotabili invece qua ). Il 26 e 27 settembre le visite saranno invece più frequenti: ogni ora dalle 10 alle 16 e si possono prenotare qua .

items.title: La Rai ha rimosso Sigfrido Ranucci dalla conduzione di “Report”
items.summary: Al suo posto sono stati scelti Giulia Presutti e Daniele Piervincenzi: una scelta sgradita agli inviati di Report, che minacciano di andarsene
items.content:
La Rai ha rimosso Sigfrido Ranucci dalla conduzione di Report , il più noto programma televisivo di giornalismo d’inchiesta in Italia, trasmesso da Rai 3. Ranucci ci lavorava come autore dal 2006 e lo conduceva dal 2017, dopo che per vent’anni lo aveva condotto la giornalista Milena Gabanelli. Il programma tornerà in tv dal prossimo 8 novembre, e la Rai ha fatto sapere che a condurlo saranno Giulia Presutti e Daniele Piervincenzi, entrambi giornalisti investigativi.

Per ora la Rai non ha dato motivazioni ufficiali per la rimozione, ma si sa che hanno a che fare con quanto emerso nelle indagini sull’attentato contro lo stesso Ranucci, compiuto a ottobre del 2025 e organizzato da Valter Lavitola, imprenditore coinvolto in diversi scandali della politica italiana degli ultimi vent’anni e molto amico di Ranucci (che non è indagato). Ranucci e la dirigenza della Rai hanno poi un rapporto conflittuale che va avanti da tempo, a prescindere dall’attentato.

Presutti è dal 2018 inviata di Report , dove si è occupata soprattutto di politica, sanità e note vicende giudiziarie. Piervincenzi invece a Report non ci ha mai lavorato, ma è alla Rai dal 2016 e sempre in programmi di approfondimento e inchiesta: nel 2017, da inviato del programma Nemo , venne aggredito con una testata in faccia da Roberto Spada, membro di una famiglia di Ostia nota per il suo coinvolgimento in diverse attività criminali. Per quell’episodio Spada fu condannato a sei anni di reclusione.

A Ranucci invece la Rai ha offerto tre possibili nuovi ruoli, che l’azienda ha definito «coerenti con il suo grado e con l’esperienza maturata in Rai». Non sono stati esplicitati, ma secondo fonti interne di diverse agenzie e giornali sarebbero un ruolo dentro RaiNews (il sito di notizie della Rai), uno al Tg3 , oppure un lavoro da corrispondente dal Cairo, in Egitto.

Ranucci ha commentato la decisione dicendo che al suo posto «sono state scelte due persone che mortificano le professionalità che per 30 anni hanno fatto la storia di Report e del servizio pubblico». Ha detto, molto enfaticamente, che al posto del programma condurrà «la battaglia più importante della mia vita per la libertà di stampa». E ancora: «lo farò per i miei figli e per i vostri, mi rifiuto di lasciare alle future generazioni questo mondo mostruoso, governato da persone mostruose e vigliacche che non tollerano il giornalismo libero e i magistrati indipendenti».

In una specie di comunicato , il gruppo degli inviati di Report ha protestato duramente contro la decisione, definita «completamente irricevibile», non tanto per la rimozione di Ranucci ma per la scelta dei sostituti: dicono che «le figure scelte non sono in alcun modo rappresentative della storia e dei valori di Report », e che la Rai non li ha coinvolti in alcun modo nella decisione. Arrivano poi a minacciare di andarsene in blocco dalla redazione del programma «nel caso in cui la Rai non intenda tornare sui propri passi».

Ranucci non è indagato nell’inchiesta sull’attentato inscenato contro di lui. La procura di Roma, competente sul caso, ritiene che non fosse a conoscenza dell’attentato e che anzi sia stato manipolato da Lavitola, che avrebbe messo in piedi tutto per accrescere la popolarità di Ranucci e spingerlo poi a entrare in politica (Lavitola si proponeva come suo consulente). Ma l’inchiesta ha mostrato anche una consuetudine tra Ranucci e Lavitola che a molti è sembrata problematica e compromettente per un giornalista dell’importanza di Ranucci, di cui Lavitola era sia fonte che confidente intimo.

Tra le altre cose, sono state pubblicate intercettazioni in cui Ranucci condivideva con Lavitola documenti interni della Rai, e altre in cui screditava pesantemente l’azienda. Diversi esponenti della destra di governo avevano chiesto che la Rai prendesse provvedimenti contro Ranucci e lo sostituisse alla conduzione di Report , accusandolo di essere fazioso, vulnerabile e inaffidabile.

Valter Lavitola arriva in procura a Roma, 8 luglio 2026 (ANSA/MASSIMO PERCOSSI)

In queste settimane Ranucci aveva più volte suggerito che la maggioranza stesse solo cercando un pretesto per censurarlo, visto che Report ha spesso fatto inchieste su politici di destra e al governo. In Italia il governo ha un’enorme influenza sulla Rai, la televisione pubblica, perché il parlamento (dove c’è un’ampia maggioranza di destra) nomina i suoi principali dirigenti e stabilisce le sue politiche di indirizzo.

Diversi esponenti dei partiti di destra al governo in queste settimane avevano chiesto la rimozione o la sospensione di Ranucci: lo aveva fatto con particolare vigore per esempio il ministro dei Trasporti Matteo Salvini, che dopo la notizia ha commentato: «Giusto così».

Il direttore dei programmi di approfondimento della Rai, Paolo Corsini, responsabile anche di Report , è ideologicamente molto vicino al governo ed è uno dei dirigenti con cui Ranucci aveva il rapporto peggiore: Corsini si era spesso lamentato col conduttore delle scelte editoriali di Report e lo accusava in sostanza di prendersela molto più spesso con il centrodestra che con il centrosinistra.

Nell’attentato di ottobre venne fatta esplodere una bomba fuori da casa di Ranucci a Campo Ascolano, una frazione del comune di Pomezia, vicino a Roma. Vennero distrutte due auto di Ranucci ma non ci furono feriti. A fine giugno erano state arrestate quattro persone con l’accusa di aver compiuto materialmente l’attentato, alcuni giorni più tardi venne indagato Lavitola, che ad agosto è stato arrestato e poi ha confessato di aver organizzato l’attentato. Lui sostiene però di averlo fatto per fare in modo che a Ranucci venisse rafforzata la scorta, temendo per la sua incolumità. È accusato del reato di strage, aggravato dal metodo mafioso.

Negli ultimi vent’anni Lavitola è stato più volte condannato per vicende giudiziarie che avevano a che fare con la politica italiana. Ranucci lo conobbe proprio occupandosi per lavoro delle vicende che lo riguardavano. In seguito i due divennero amici, e Lavitola fu una fonte di Ranucci per alcuni suoi lavori giornalistici.

items.title: Apple TV aumenta ancora negli Stati Uniti: in Italia c’è calma piatta da 3 anni
items.summary: Negli Stati Uniti Apple TV è al quarto aumento in quattro anni. Noi per ora ne abbiamo saltati due ... Leggi tutto
items.content:
Apple ha aumentato ancora il prezzo di Apple TV negli Stati Uniti, e anche in Brasile, Cile e Messico; questi ultimi citati da MacRumors .

Sale anche Apple One Individual , il pacchetto che comprende Apple TV e altri servizi dell’azienda, con il prezzo mensile che passa da 19,95 a 21,95 dollari.

Per Apple TV è il quarto aumento in quattro anni negliu USA. Partito nel 2019 a 4,99 dollari al mese, il servizio di streaming video di Cupertino ora costa il triplo. Dopo il passaggio a 6,99 dollari e quello a 9,99 dollari dell’ottobre del 2023, negli Stati Uniti erano già arrivati i 12,99 dollari nell’agosto dell’anno scorso. Non contenti, un anno dopo è scattato un altro rincaro del 15,4%, anche se bisogna considerare che per il pubblico americano è stata compresa l'attuale stagione di F1 in streaming.

In Italia e negli altri mercati dell’Unione Europea che adottano l’euro, invece, il canone è rimasto incredibilmente fermo a 9,99 euro al mese da 3 anni . L’ultimo aumento risale all’ottobre 2023, quando il prezzo salì anche per noi da 6,99 a 9,99 euro. In questi mercati sono quindi saltati i rincari a stelle strisce del 2025 e 2026, almeno a oggi.

Indipendentemente dalla penetrazione del servizio in Italia, Apple TV avrebbe ancora un certo margine di aumento se rapportato con la proposta di Netflix, che nel Bel Paese è a 13,99 euro per il piano Standard euro, ma senza 4K HDR incluso.

items.title: BYD rallenta nel primo semestre: ricavi e utili in calo, ma l’estero cresce del 68%
items.summary: Le vendite complessive di veicoli elettrificati sono scese del 15,7%. Quasi un’auto su due viene ormai venduta fuori dalla Cina ... Leggi tutto
items.content:
BYD ha chiuso il primo semestre di quest'anno con ricavi e utile netto in calo, penalizzata soprattutto dalla debolezza delle vendite automobilistiche sul mercato domestico e da perdite legate ai cambi valutari.

Nei primi sei mesi dell’anno il fatturato è sceso del 7,13% su base annua, fermandosi a 344,82 miliardi di yuan, circa 50,9 miliardi di dollari. L’utile netto attribuibile agli azionisti è diminuito ancora di più, del 20,54%, a 12,33 miliardi di yuan.

Nei primi sei mesi del 2026, BYD ha esportato circa 792.000 veicoli nel semestre, con una crescita del 67,8% rispetto allo stesso periodo del 2025. Le vendite internazionali hanno così rappresentato circa il 44% del totale.

La divisione automobilistica e i prodotti collegati hanno generato 275,34 miliardi di yuan di ricavi, in calo dell’8,98% e pari a quasi l’80% del fatturato complessivo del gruppo. A pesare è stato soprattutto il calo dei volumi. BYD ha venduto 1.808.511 veicoli elettrificati nel primo semestre, il 15,72% in meno rispetto a un anno prima. La flessione si è però ridotta nettamente nel secondo trimestre: tra aprile e giugno le vendite sono scese del 3,24% su base annua, contro il -30,01% registrato nei primi tre mesi dell’anno.

Nel secondo trimestre BYD ha venduto all’estero 471.091 veicoli, con un aumento dell’82,46% rispetto allo stesso periodo del 2025 e del 46,68% rispetto al trimestre precedente. Questa espansione ha aiutato anche la redditività: il profitto lordo complessivo è sceso del 2,81% a 64,99 miliardi di yuan, ma il margine lordo è salito dal 18,01% al 18,85%. In altre parole, BYD ha venduto meno veicoli nel complesso, ma una quota crescente delle consegne è arrivata da mercati internazionali e da prodotti con una redditività migliore.

Un contributo positivo, infatti, è arrivato da Denza, Fang Cheng Bao e Yangwang. Le vendite combinate dei tre marchi più costosi del gruppo sono aumentate del 61% su base annua e hanno raggiunto il 12,8% delle vendite complessive di auto passeggeri.

A luglio - quindi primo mese del secondo semestre - BYD ha venduto 419.211 veicoli, il 21,76% in più rispetto allo stesso mese del 2025, il terzo mese consecutivo di crescita. Ancora una volta, il contributo dell’estero è stato decisivo: le vendite internazionali di auto passeggeri e pickup hanno raggiunto il record di 179.841 unità, in aumento del 124,3% su base annua e pari a circa il 43% del totale del mese.

items.title: L'autore dei video leak di GTA VI è scappato con i soldi
items.summary: Appena prima della pubblicazione dell'anteprima ufficiale di GTA VI, Cyberleek ha incassato i proventi accumulati dal trading della memecoin pubblicizzata insieme ad ogni video non autorizzato ed è sparito dalla circolazione ... Leggi tutto
items.content:
Qualcuno evidentemente aveva persino creduto che l'hacker (o gruppo) autore della pubblicazione dei 15 video pirata di GTA VI fosse davvero un paladino contro le ingiustizie dell'odierna industria videoludica, comprando e scambiando la memecoin pubblicizzata ad ogni leak. Dopo tutto Cyberleek, questo il nome del pirata informatico, aveva bruciato tutti i suoi token $CYBERLEEK per dimostrare la propria buona fede; cosa poteva mai andare storto? E invece Cyberleek ha incassato circa 270.000 dollari di commissioni sulle transazioni ed è uscito di scena , guarda caso poche ore prima della pubblicazione dell'anteprima ufficiale di GTA VI, ben sapendo che avrebbe fatto calare l'interesse verso i suoi leak, lasciando colare a picco il valore della memecoin, a danno di tutti quelli che ci erano cascati.

La truffa ha sfruttato l'attesa per GTA VI per pompare il valore dei token $CYBERLEEK creati appositamente per l'operazione. Usualmente, negli scam sulle memecoin i truffatori scappano svuotando i propri wallet dopo aver pompato al massimo il valore dei token. In questo caso è stata utilizzata una tattica diversa, sfruttando le commissioni generate da ogni transazione per fare cassa , che si sono susseguite in grande volume ad ogni pubblicazione, appositamente centellinata, di nuovi video. Il token aveva raggiunto un massimo di 0,034 dollari per una capitalizzazione di oltre 23 milioni di dollari. Dopo che Cyberleek ha scambiato i token delle commissioni in SOL (la criptomoneta della blockchain Solana), distribuendoli su vari wallet, il valore dei $CYBERLEEK è crollato, e attualmente sta a 0,00348 dollari.

Secondo le indagini effettuate da un membro della community di gtaforums.com , l'autore della truffa avrebbe investito 29.000 dollari per creare il token e il sito legato ai leak. Significa che in tutto l'attività ha fruttato meno di 250.000 dollari. Considerando le attenzioni attirate su di sé e il fatto che gli strumenti utilizzati non sono impossibili da tracciare, ci si chiede se il bottino sia commisurato ai rischi corsi. Sempre che questa sia effettivamente la parola fine della vicenda.
